title_original: ‘Focker In-Law’ review: Ariana Grande joins Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro for strained fourth installment of comedy franchise
excerpt_original: Skyler Gisondo and Teri Polo also star in the hit-and-miss sequel, rolling out globally from November 25

blocks.text: Twenty-six years after the start of the franchise, Focker In-Law places Ben Stiller’s uptight dad in the same position that Robert De Niro’s disapproving future father-in-law was in original movie Meet The Parents – having to accept that his grown up child wants to marry someone he doesn’t approve of. That role reversal gives this sequel a clever central idea, and Stiller does his best to generate laughs from the klutzy, painfully insecure Greg Focker. But despite Ariana Grande’s game performance as the incoming fiancee, this hit-and-miss fourth instalment further demonstrates how strained this once-fresh comedic presence has become.
Quickly devolves into contrivances and nonsensical behaviour

Opening November 25 in the UK and US, this rare studio comedy is perfectly positioned for the holiday season. The last installment, 2010’s Little Fockers , collected $311 million worldwide, and the reteaming of Stiller and De Niro should lead to another lucrative chapter. Pop star and Wicked sensation Grande will only add extra commercial oomph.

Happy husband and father Greg travels with his family to see his father-in-law Jack Byrnes (De Niro), who’s having a party to celebrate his 80th birthday. But Greg is especially excited because he will finally meet his beloved son Henry’s (Skyler Gisondo) girlfriend Olivia (Grande), who will also be attending the soiree.

But on the plane to Jack’s, Greg has a convolutedly awkward encounter with a fellow passenger that nearly leads to him being arrested — only later learning that the passenger is actually Olivia, a former FBI hostage negotiator who now works as an executive coach. Greg is suitably embarrassed, but he becomes frustrated once the famously grumpy Jack instantly takes a liking to Olivia, showing her a respect he never demonstrated toward Greg – who has always desperately wanted Jack to like him.

John Hamburg, who was one of the writers on the first three films, serves as screenwriter and director on Focker In-Law , which boasts a livelier, funnier tone than the aggressively juvenile previous two sequels. It helps that the new picture has a couple potentially rich comedic conceits, including the fact that Greg resents Olivia because she is not being grilled by Jack the way that he was when he was planning to marry Jack’s daughter Pam (Teri Polo). Also amusing is Greg’s realization that he is older now than Jack was when the two men first met. Suddenly, Greg finds himself in the same situation Jack was all those years ago, trying to keep Henry from proposing because he feels threatened by Olivia’s assertiveness and ease in the world.

In Meet the Parents , Stiller smartly portrayed a goodhearted but ineffectual young man instantly intimidated by Jack’s background as a CIA agent, which set the stage for a humorous clash. Focker In-Law continues to mine that premise, except this time Greg feels outclassed by a woman — albeit one who has similar life experience to Jack which, to the older man’s mind, makes her more impressive than his meek son-in-law. Much of the new film’s humour stems from Greg hurting or humiliating himself through elaborate set pieces that rely on slapstick or comic misunderstandings. But although Stiller remains an ace straight man, slowly simmering as everything blows up in his face (sometimes literally), Hamburg struggles to give his star enough choice material.

Likewise, De Niro leans on his trademark gruffness as Jack. But the spark that made De Niro’s Meet The Parents performance so entertaining — essentially, the fearsome force known for Taxi Driver and Raging Bull playing the worst-case scenario of the judgmental father-in-law — has long since become predictable. What works better are Greg’s showdowns with Olivia, in which she clearly has the upper hand. Grande-Butera brings just the right amount of silent superiority, rendering Olivia has someone who wants to get to know Henry’s family but, unlike Greg, is comfortable in her own skin.

Despite the occasional funny sequence or bizarre running gag, the plot quickly devolves into contrivances and nonsensical behaviour in which the characters keep lying to each other when simply telling the truth would resolve most of their problems. Rather than exploiting the relatable humour that derives from the realistic tensions between in-laws — which helped make Meet The Parents such an enduring comedy — Focker In-Law mostly goes for outrageous gags and ridiculous scenarios.
Production companies: Tribeca, Red Hour Films, Delirious Media, Particular Pictures
International distribution: Paramount Pictures / US distribution: Universal Pictures
Producers: Jane Rosenthal, Robert De Niro, Ben Stiller, John Lesher, Jay Roach, John Hamburg
Screenplay: John Hamburg, story by John Hamburg and Ilana Glazer & Austen Earl, based on characters created by Greg Glienna & Mary Ruth Clarke
Main cast: Robert De Niro, Ben Stiller, Owen Wilson, Teri Polo, Blythe Danner, Skyler Gisondo, Beanie Feldstein, Eduardo Franco, Ariana Grande
